title: How Are We to Pray? The Rule of Prayer
speaker: Mr. Alex Lyro

outline.title: Reverent Apprehension of God's Majesty
subpoints: Prayer requires an 'awful' (awe-filled) realization of God's greatness
God is not merely loving but majestic, infinite, and separate from creation
Reverence is the first rule of true prayer

outline.title: A Deep Sense of Unworthiness
subpoints: Recognizing the chasm between Creator and creature
Acknowledging that we have no inherent claim on God's mercy

outline.title: Awareness of Necessities and Sins
subpoints: Honest consciousness of physical and spiritual needs
Contrast between the Pharisee's boasting and the Tax Collector's humility
Confession of sin is prerequisite for receiving grace

outline.title: Penitent and Thankful Hearts
subpoints: Repentance involves hating sin and turning from it, not just confessing
Internal heart change ('rend your heart') vs. outward ritual
Thanksgiving should saturate all prayer, not just be a perfunctory opening

summary:
In this Sunday school session, Mr. Alex Lyro continues the study of the Westminster Larger Catechism, focusing on Questions 185 and 186 regarding the manner and rule of prayer. The primary text for discussion is Question 185, which outlines the necessary dispositions of the heart for true prayer. The teaching emphasizes that prayer must begin with an 'awful apprehension' of God's majesty, defined not as terror but as reverential awe. This reverence acknowledges God's infinite greatness and separation from creation, countering a modern tendency to view God solely through the lens of His love. Drawing on Hebrews 12 and Ecclesiastes 5, the lesson asserts that recognizing God's holiness is the foundation for acceptable worship.

The session further explores the necessity of humility, described as a 'deep sense of our own unworthiness.' Using the example of Abraham in Genesis 18, the speaker illustrates that true prayer involves recognizing one's status as 'dust and ashes' before the Almighty. This humility extends to an honest awareness of one's necessities and sins. The parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector (Luke 18) is used to contrast self-righteousness with the humble confession required to approach God. The lesson stresses that without acknowledging sin, the grace of forgiveness and growth cannot be fully received, as illustrated by the metaphor of healing a wound only after it is admitted.

Finally, the teaching addresses the need for penitent and thankful hearts. Penitence is defined not as outward ritual or self-punishment, but as an internal rending of the heart, turning away from sin with a desire to forsake it, as commanded in Joel 2. Thanksgiving is presented not as a perfunctory opening line, but as a saturation of the entire prayer life, supported by references to 1 Thessalonians, Colossians, and Philippians. The session concludes by emphasizing that these dispositions—reverence, humility, confession, repentance, and gratitude—are essential for praying in a manner that glorifies God.
